lesson.title: How Much Can You Get Away With? T-Procedures and Non-Normal Data
lesson.summary: T-procedures are fairly robust to violations of normality, especially as sample size grows, but that robustness does not extend to outliers or to violations of independence, which can distort results at any sample size.
lesson.body:
A statistical procedure is called robust to a violation of some condition if the procedure keeps behaving close to its advertised way even when that condition is not perfectly met. T-procedures turn out to be fairly robust to non-normality, particularly as the sample size grows, thanks to the Central Limit Theorem's effect on the sampling distribution of the mean, the same idea behind the normality condition in conditions for t-procedures. The bigger the sample, the closer the sampling distribution of the mean gets to normal, regardless of the shape of the population it came from.

A widely used rule of thumb translates that idea into rough sample-size guidance. For small samples, roughly under 15 observations, only trust a t-procedure if the data themselves look reasonably symmetric, single-peaked, and free of outliers. For moderate samples, roughly 15 to 40, t-procedures generally hold up unless the data show strong skewness or outliers. For large samples, roughly 40 or more, t-procedures tend to be trustworthy even when the underlying data are clearly skewed, because the Central Limit Theorem has done enough work by then. Treat these as rough guideposts rather than a strict law, actual judgment about the specific data in front of you still matters.

But robustness to non-normality is not the same thing as robustness to outliers, and that distinction matters a lot. The sample mean and sample standard deviation, the two ingredients every t-procedure runs on, are both extremely sensitive to extreme values, exactly the concern raised in outlier. Consider 8 measured task-completion times, in minutes: 12, 14, 13, 15, 12, 16, 14, 52. With all eight values included, the sum is 148 and the mean is 148 divided by 8, or 18.5. Remove the single outlier, 52, and the remaining 7 values sum to 96, giving a mean of 96 divided by 7, about 13.71. One value out of eight shifted the mean by nearly 5 minutes, and it would inflate the standard deviation similarly. No amount of sample size fixes that kind of distortion, a single unusual point can dominate a t-procedure whether n is 8 or 800.

The practical takeaway: always look at the data, most simply with a dotplot, boxplot, or stemplot, before running a t-procedure, checking specifically for outliers and strong skew, not just relying on a sample size cutoff as a blanket excuse. And remember that robustness only covers the normality condition. It does nothing to rescue a study built on a biased sampling method or on observations that were not actually independent, no sample size, however large, repairs those problems.
